summary: Describes an extension to Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) object mappings that lets an organization be assigned to any existing object, such as a domain, host, or contact, and to future objects. It works with the organization mapping in RFC 8543. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: This lets you stick an organization label onto a domain record, like putting a name tag on a box to show who it belongs to.

questions: what is the epp organization extension
how to assign a reseller to a domain in epp
what does orgext id role mean
subtitle: An EPP extension that attaches organizations, such as a reseller or privacy proxy, to domains, hosts and contacts.

tldr.problem: Registrars, resellers, DNS service operators and privacy proxies all take part in domain registration, but EPP objects had no standard way to point to them.
tldr.mechanism: The extension adds orgext:id elements, each with a role attribute, to the create, update and info exchanges of existing EPP object mappings, referring to organization objects defined in RFC 8543.
tldr.outcome: Domains, hosts and contacts can be linked to organizations by role, with at most one organization per role per object. It is a Proposed Standard registered in the EPP extension registry.

today: RFC 8544 is a Proposed Standard, published in April 2019, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. It works together with the organization mapping in RFC 8543.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Many parties take part in the domain registration business, including registrars, resellers, DNS service operators and privacy proxies. The Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) already supports these as "organization" entities through RFC 8543.

This RFC supplies the missing link. It associates any EPP object, such as a domain from RFC 5731, a host from RFC 5732 or a contact from RFC 5733, with an organization entity. The examples use domain objects; hosts and contacts can be extended the same way. Organization identifiers MUST be known to the server before the organization can be associated with an object.
sections.eli5: Companies already have their own cards in the system. This document explains how to clip a company's card onto a domain, host or contact.

sections.title: The Organization Identifier and Role
sections.content:
The extension adds one main element, <orgext:id>. It holds the identifier of an organization, which refers to the <org:id> element from RFC 8543. Organization objects are identified by a server-unique identifier.

Each <orgext:id> has a required role attribute giving the relationship of the organization to the object, for example reseller or privacyproxy in the RFC's examples. The list of role values comes from Section 7.3 of RFC 8543. An object MUST have at most one associated organization ID for any given role value.

The extension namespace is urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:epp:orgext-1.0, with the prefix orgext. Implementations MUST NOT depend on the prefix and should use a namespace-aware XML parser.
sections.eli5: Each tag has two parts: which company, and what job it does for this domain. A domain can have only one company per job.

sections.title: Create and Info Commands
sections.content:
For <create>, the command MUST carry an <extension> element holding an <orgext:create> element, which contains one or more <orgext:id> elements. No new elements are added to the create response. The server returns an error if the command cannot be processed.

For <info>, no elements are added to the command, but the response <extension> SHOULD contain an <orgext:infData> element when the object has data for this extension, based on server policy. It holds zero or more <orgext:id> elements, so an object with no organization gets an empty infData.

The <check>, <transfer> query, <delete> and <renew> commands and responses get no new elements. After a successful transfer of an object with an assigned organization, how the organization is handled depends on its role and on server policy.
sections.eli5: When you make a new domain you can attach company tags. When you ask for information about a domain, the answer lists the tags, or shows an empty list if there are none.

sections.title: The Update Command
sections.content:
An <update> command carries an <orgext:update> element with at least one of three optional children, each holding one or more <orgext:id> elements:

  • <orgext:add> adds roles that do not yet exist. The identifier MUST be non-empty, and the server SHOULD check that the role does not already exist.
  • <orgext:rem> removes roles. The identifier MAY be empty, and the server SHOULD check that the role (and the identifier, if given) exists.
  • <orgext:chg> replaces the existing identifier for a role. The server SHOULD check that the role exists.

If any listed role already exists in an add, or does not exist in a remove or change, the object is not changed at all. The server SHOULD signal this with a 2305 error response code.
sections.eli5: To change tags you can add a new one, take one off, or swap one for another. If one of the changes does not make sense, nothing changes at all.

sections.title: Formal Syntax and Internationalization
sections.content:
The extension is defined with an XML Schema. Its root elements are create, update and infData. All use an orgIdType, a token with a required role attribute. The create and the add, remove and change children require one or more ids; infData allows zero or more.

EPP is represented in XML, so Unicode is natively supported. UTF-8 is RECOMMENDED. The elements in this document inherit the internationalization conventions of the domain and core protocol structures they extend.
sections.eli5: There is a strict form that spells out exactly how a tag must be written, so computers can check it automatically.

sections.title: IANA and Security
sections.content:
IANA assigned the namespace URI urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:epp:orgext-1.0 and the schema URI urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:epp:orgext-1.0. The extension is registered in the EPP extension registry from RFC 7451 with status Active, for any TLD.

On security, the extension adds no other security services and no considerations beyond those of RFC 5730, RFC 5731, RFC 5732 and RFC 5733, or those caused by the protocol layers EPP uses.
sections.eli5: The extension has been written down in an official list of EPP add-ons. It does not add any new safety worries beyond those EPP already has.
